verses.text: Jacob lifted up his eyes, and looked, and, behold, Esau was coming, and with him four hundred men. He divided the children between Leah, Rachel, and the two servants.
He put the servants and their children in front, Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear.
He himself passed over in front of them, and bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother.
Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept.
He lifted up his eyes, and saw the women and the children; and said, “Who are these with you?” He said, “The children whom God has graciously given your servant.”
Then the servants came near with their children, and they bowed themselves.
Leah also and her children came near, and bowed themselves. After them, Joseph came near with Rachel, and they bowed themselves.
Esau said, “What do you mean by all this company which I met?” Jacob said, “To find favor in the sight of my lord.”
Esau said, “I have enough, my brother; let that which you have be yours.”
Jacob said, “Please, no, if I have now found favor in your sight, then receive my present at my hand, because I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God, and you were pleased with me.
Please take the gift that I brought to you, because God has dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough.” He urged him, and he took it.
Esau said, “Let us take our journey, and let us go, and I will go before you.”
Jacob said to him, “My lord knows that the children are tender, and that the flocks and herds with me have their young, and if they overdrive them one day, all the flocks will die.

Please let my lord pass over before his servant, and I will lead on gently, according to the pace of the livestock that are before me and according to the pace of the children, until I come to my lord to Seir.”
Esau said, “Let me now leave with you some of the folk who are with me.” He said, “Why? Let me find favor in the sight of my lord.”
So Esau returned that day on his way to Seir.
Jacob traveled to Succoth, built himself a house, and made shelters for his livestock. Therefore the name of the place is called Succoth.
Jacob came in peace to the city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Paddan Aram; and encamped before the city.
He bought the parcel of ground where he had spread his tent, at the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for one hundred pieces of money.
He erected an altar there, and called it El Elohe Israel.

footnotes.content: Here is Jacob, the one who once fled from Esau in fear, now looking up to see him coming with four hundred men. I have known that tightening in the chest when we must meet someone we have wronged. Yet even here, the Lord is bringing the estranged brothers toward each other once more, though only He knows how it will end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob carefully places his family, putting those he would most shield furthest from danger and Rachel and Joseph last of all. I understand a father's anxious calculation. But the God who has kept this family through Laban is now about to show them that His care runs deeper than any human strategy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Before his servants or his family, Jacob goes ahead alone and bows seven times as he draws near. Once he had grabbed his brother's heel, now he is content to take the lowest place. I have learned that when our hearts begin to bend in repentance, it is often the Lord softening them to walk in humility.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau does not draw his sword, he runs to meet him. He embraces him, falls on his neck, and kisses him, and both weep. After so many years of grief, mercy comes unearned. Our God delights to turn a day we feared into a day of undeserved kindness to those who once were enemies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau asks about the women and children, and Jacob answers that they are the children whom God has graciously given his servant. After all his scheming, Jacob now sees clearly: none of these blessings are his by right. Like him, I must learn to call every good gift what it truly is — the grace of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One by one, the servants and their children draw near and bow themselves. What Jacob feared would be an ambush has become an act of courtesy between brothers restored. The Lord often answers our worst fears with kindness we would never have dared to ask for.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Leah and her children bow, and at last Rachel and Joseph do the same. For a man who had once pitted his affections, it is good to see this broken family brought together in peace. The God of reconciliation is not ashamed to heal what human sin has torn apart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau inquires about the whole company Jacob sent ahead, and Jacob answers simply: to find favor in the sight of my lord. Though his words are humble, his heart is cautious still. I know that feeling — when mercy has come, we still tremble to trust it fully.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau refuses to take it as payment, saying he already has enough. What a contrast to Jacob's lifelong fear of lack. The brother once robbed of birthright now speaks as one content, while the one who grasped so much is learning to receive grace instead of buying peace. Our God alone makes us truly rich.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob pleads with Esau to take the gift, for he has seen his face as one sees the face of God, and Esau was pleased with him. To behold mercy where we expected wrath is to see something of the very countenance of our Lord. How much more true is this for those who, through Christ, behold the face of God in full forgiveness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob insists, for God has dealt graciously with him and he has enough. After wrestling at Peniel, he knows it to be true. I find it slow to learn as well: peace is not built by what we give to earn it, but rests in the fact that our God has already given us all things in mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau offers to travel together and go ahead to protect the way. It is a kind offer from a brother whose heart the Lord has truly changed. We ought to give thanks when God gives us restored relationships, even if they only last a season for His wise purposes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob gently refuses, speaking of the tenderness of the children and the young ones among the flocks and herds. The man who once drove hard bargains now drives gently for the sake of the weak. When the Lord softens our hearts, our strength begins to be used to care for others rather than to grasp for ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob will go at the pace of the little ones until he comes to Esau at Seir. This is wisdom born of love, not cowardice. Our good Shepherd does the same for us: He leads His flock gently, bearing the lambs in His bosom, and going slowly with those who are weak.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau offers to leave some of his men to help, but Jacob humbly declines, content simply to find favor. After striving so long, he is learning to rest in what God has already done. There is a quiet joy in needing less from man when we are learning to trust the Lord for all we need.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau turns back toward Seir, and the brothers part in peace. We do not see them meet again in this life, yet God has given them this gift of reconciliation. Sometimes the Lord heals enough for us to part in kindness, entrusting the rest to Him who judges and heals all things.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob goes to Succoth, builds a house for himself, and shelters for his livestock, and the place is called Succoth, meaning 'shelters'. After years of tents and fleeing, he is building again. Yet he will soon move on to Shechem; even the home we build reminds us that this earth is not yet our lasting rest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob comes in peace to Shechem in the land of Canaan, the land God promised to Abraham and Isaac. The word 'in peace' is precious after so much turmoil. I have found that true peace is not the absence of trouble, but the presence of the God who has brought us safely thus far.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob buys the parcel of ground where he pitched his tent from the children of Hamor, Shechem's father, for one hundred pieces of money. For the first time, the sojourner owns a piece of the promised land. It is but a small plot, yet it is a foretaste: the day is coming when all God's people will possess the whole inheritance in full.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There Jacob erects an altar and calls it El Elohe Israel, meaning 'God, the God of Israel'. After so long, the struggler names God as the God of Israel. I, too, must learn to stop clinging to the old name and trust that the God who wrestled with me is the same God who has made me His own through our greater Redeemer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
